claims.text: The starting material is a W–Cu composite containing discrete W particles or interconnected W ligaments within a Cu matrix.
Adding 1–2 wt% Ni to W–Cu can overcome phase separation and interfacial void formation.
Ni can be introduced into the W–Cu composite by ball-milling followed by high-temperature sintering or infiltration.
W-based plasma-facing materials and Cu-based heat sinks operate under high temperature, high heat flux, and intense neutron irradiation.
The relevant service heat load is approximately 10–20 MW/m2.
The relevant service environment includes concurrent neutron and ion irradiation.
Added Ni atoms will segregate at the W–Cu interface.
Interfacial Ni segregation will stabilize the W–Cu interface and inhibit deleterious interfacial reactions.
Ni doping lowers the interfacial energy of W–Cu.
Lower interfacial energy limits interfacial void nucleation.
Ni suppresses excessive W–Cu phase separation during high-heat-flux and irradiation exposure.
Reduced void formation and phase separation preserve continuous thermal-conduction pathways.
The Ni-doped composite will have lower interfacial porosity than an equivalently processed undoped W–Cu composite.
The Ni-doped composite will retain higher thermal conductivity in service than an equivalently processed undoped W–Cu composite.
Ni additions above approximately 2 wt% may form secondary phases or degrade thermal properties.
The intervention is applicable to W–Cu heat-sink and plasma-facing applications under high heat flux and moderate neutron or ion irradiation.
The optimal Ni concentration and processing window have not been fully validated under long-duration reactor irradiation.
Similar or worse interfacial integrity or thermal-conductivity degradation in Ni-doped samples relative to undoped controls would falsify the hypothesis.
